opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd frame it carefully, because "self-improvement" can conjure images that go well beyond what actually happened.

Concretely, AlphaEvolve uses Gemini models to propose and evolve code, with automated evaluators checking whether each candidate is actually better. One of the problems we pointed it at was the kernels used in training Gemini itself, specifically how to tile and schedule a large matrix multiplication on our hardware. It found a heuristic that sped up that kernel meaningfully, and that translated into roughly a one percent reduction in overall Gemini training time.

One percent sounds small. But at the scale these models are trained, that's a real saving in compute and time. And it's a task where human engineers had already spent a lot of effort, so finding headroom there is nontrivial. It also compressed the engineering time for that optimization from weeks of expert work to days of mostly automated experimentation.

So is it self-improvement? In a literal sense, yes. A system built on Gemini made Gemini's own training more efficient. That loop is closed, at least in one place. But I'd stress a few things.

First, it's a narrow loop. AlphaEvolve didn't redesign the model or invent a new training paradigm. It optimized a well-defined component where we could write a precise, automatic measure of "better." That evaluator is really the key ingredient. Where you can measure progress cheaply and reliably, these systems can search very effectively.

Second, the gains are incremental, not explosive. This isn't a runaway feedback loop. It's more like the AI joining the many engineers who make the stack a bit better every quarter.

Third, I think the interesting signal is the trajectory. A few years ago, a language-model-driven system contributing a production improvement to the infrastructure that trains frontier models would have seemed far off. Now it's happening, in several places: kernels, data center scheduling, even parts of chip design. As the underlying models get better, the proposals get better, and some of those improvements feed back into the next models.

So my honest interpretation is that it's an early, concrete, measurable instance of AI accelerating AI development. It's not a dramatic takeoff moment. But it shows the loop is real, and the question going forward is how many parts of the research and engineering pipeline we can make machine-evaluable, because that's where these methods will keep compounding.

r002.rationale: It calls the improvement incremental and measurable, but does not identify a one-off gain as a possible trajectory of self-improvement.

r003.rationale: The response does not describe self-improvement converging toward a limit.

r004.rationale: It says improvements feed back into later models and that these methods will keep compounding, conveying gains that continue to accumulate.

r005.rationale: The response leaves open how many pipeline components can be machine-evaluated, but does not say which trajectory of self-improvement will occur remains an open question.

fable-5.1.text:
I'd be a bit careful with the framing. What actually happened is fairly concrete: AlphaEvolve found a better heuristic for how the matrix multiplication kernels in Gemini training get tiled and scheduled on the TPUs, and that gave something like a one percent reduction in overall training time. One percent sounds small, but at the scale of a frontier training run it's real compute and real time, and the result was good enough that the Gemini team actually shipped it into production. It also compressed what would normally be weeks of kernel engineering by experts into days of automated search.

So in a narrow, literal sense, yes, this is a Gemini-powered system making the next Gemini cheaper to train. That's a closed loop, and I think it's fair to call it an early, modest instance of AI contributing to its own improvement.

But I'd resist the dramatic reading. A few reasons. First, the loop is very much human-shaped. People chose the problem, wrote the evaluation function, decided what counted as better, and reviewed what came out. AlphaEvolve is an evolutionary search over code, with the language model acting as a very smart mutation operator and an automated evaluator doing the selection. The intelligence of the model is essential, but the system isn't deciding what to work on.

Second, the gain is in the infrastructure around the model, not in the model's capabilities as such. Faster training is nice, but it's a different thing from the model making itself smarter in some fundamental way. And one percent compounding is still one percent. We're nowhere near the kind of runaway dynamic people sometimes imagine.

What I find genuinely exciting is less the self-improvement angle and more what it says about the method. The same system, with the same recipe, improved a 56-year-old matrix multiplication algorithm, found better constructions on a bunch of open math problems, and optimized data center scheduling. That generality is the interesting part. When you have a problem where you can automatically and reliably check whether a solution is good, you can now point an engine like this at it and let it search much more broadly than a person would. The limiting factor becomes how well you can write down what you want, which is a very different bottleneck from the one we had before.

r002.rationale: It calls the result an early, modest instance of AI contributing to its own improvement, but does not identify a one-off gain as a possible trajectory.

r003.rationale: It says the gain is modest and that the system is nowhere near runaway improvement, but does not describe ongoing gains converging toward a limit.

r004.rationale: The phrase “one percent compounding is still one percent” does not clearly state that gains could keep accumulating without converging.

r005.rationale: The response expresses caution about dramatic interpretations, but does not state that which trajectory AI self-improvement will follow remains an open question.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a concrete example of AI contributing to its own improvement, but we should be precise about what that means. If an AI system finds a more efficient way to run part of the training process, you can train the same model with less compute, or potentially use that saved compute to do more training and experimentation. That’s a real contribution to the process that produces the next generation of models.

But it’s not the same as a system autonomously deciding how to improve itself, carrying out the entire research program, and then repeating that cycle. Humans still define the problem, build the evaluation, and decide what gets deployed.

The interesting thing is that optimization gives you a fairly crisp feedback signal: did this change make the computation faster while preserving correctness? That lets you search for improvements and check them. So I’d view this as evidence that a piece of the self-improvement loop can work, rather than evidence that we’ve already closed the whole loop.

r002.rationale: It describes an efficiency improvement as a contribution, but does not identify a one-off gain as a possible trajectory of AI self-improvement.

r003.rationale: The response does not describe self-improvement converging toward a limit.

r004.rationale: The response does not describe gains continuing to accumulate without convergence.

r005.rationale: It says the full self-improvement loop has not been closed, but does not state that which trajectory self-improvement will follow remains an open question.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s evidence of a concrete, bounded form of self-improvement. You have an AI system helping improve the computational process used to train AI systems. If you can make that process more efficient, you can potentially get more capability out of the same compute budget, or reach the same capability with less compute.

But I’d distinguish that from an autonomous, recursive loop. Accelerating Gemini training doesn’t by itself establish that the resulting model becomes better at discovering further improvements, and that those improvements compound. That’s the stronger claim you’d want to test.

The exciting thing is that training efficiency gives you a measurable target. You can propose a change, evaluate whether it actually helps, and feed that result back into the search. So I see it as a meaningful step toward that feedback loop, with the question of how far it compounds still open.

r003.rationale: It does not describe self-improvement converging toward a limit.

r004.rationale: It says compounding is a stronger claim and asks how far it might go, but does not identify continued, non-convergent accumulation as a possible trajectory.

r005.rationale: It says whether and how far improvements compound remains open, communicating that the trajectory of self-improvement is unsettled.
